title: Breaking And Entering: Dry Cleaning On Their Latest Album 'Secret Love'
transcript:
A Breaking and Entering conversation with Dry Cleaning about Secret Love, broadcast on 22 January 2026.

They just did a UK tour, playing songs from the new album — it came out at the start of January — for the first time. This is Flo responding to how the shows have been going.

Really good. We were saying yesterday that people seem to have kind of gelled with them really quickly. And sometimes you play new stuff for a long, long time before you get that kind of recognition from the audience, and before people really kind of start to feel it. But we found that super quickly with these songs. I'm not sure why. Maybe there's an immediacy to them that's a bit more kind of sticky than the songs on Stumpwork or something like that. Those are kind of more slow-burn kind of vibe. But it's been great. It's been really nice.

Yeah, Lewis, that's actually a really interesting point. I guess your songs typically don't have conventional choruses or obvious hooks. I mean, there are maybe some more conventional-esque choruses on this record. Lewis, can you talk about when you finished making this record? Did you have a sense that it would be more immediate for listeners?

No, it's really hard to judge. It's almost impossible to judge how it kind of goes down. Your expectations always get flipped. So something that you think was going to work in the studio might not work in the studio, kind of works live. Something that works in the studio doesn't always work live.

So it's always a pleasant surprise, and it's one of my favourite things about the whole recording process, where your expectations flip, but also how you hear the songs flips as well. So when you demo a song, it sounds to us a certain way. And then when we show it to someone, it instantly sounds different. When we record it, it actually sounds different. But then when it becomes public, it sounds different again. And you kind of, like, submit it to the world, and then the song sounds different to yourself too.

Yeah, that is super interesting. And I guess, I suppose this record's fairly collaborative. Internally, you seem to be a very collaborative band, and then sort of demoing with Gilla Band and working with Cate Le Bon, from what I've read. Also sort of getting some input from Jason from Sleaford Mods. Flo, is, like, sort of reaching out to people outside the band pretty helpful for gauging whether songs are working or making an impression on people?

It can be. It kind of tells you quite interesting things sometimes. We sort of showed our demos to Jason, and he would immediately pick up on certain lines or just get really excited about certain lines. Like, kind of, he'd either laugh out loud, or he'd want to hear it again, or he'd say, 'Oh, you should say that again at the end of the song,' or, 'That should come at the start of a verse. It's such a great line.'

And it's not that I necessarily followed that advice word for word, but it's just really interesting because obviously the lyrics are so personal to me. Things that mean a lot to me, or things that I find really funny, are not always the same as somebody else coming to it totally fresh. So it's just kind of intriguing. It's like an experiment or something. It's like a lab or something, where watching his reactions was so interesting and quite freeing in a way.

It really reduced the pressure somehow just to show it to somebody, but someone who I knew kind of knew what it was like to write and perform a little bit in the way that I do. Yeah, he was a really valuable person to chat to, actually.

That's interesting you used the word pressure. Did you feel much pressure having to make this album?

I think amongst ourselves, we're always trying to impress each other, which is a bit of a cliche, but it is true. I don't think we often think about the audience necessarily until this point. It's always like you want to — I mean, it sounds so kind of wholesome — but you want to do your best, because we're each just striving quite a bit to write good stuff and to push ourselves. And so you want to meet that level.

I mean, it would be — sorry, Lewis.

No, I was gonna say there's never a moment where it's kind of, 'Now we start writing.' We're kind of always kind of jamming, and there's always such a bank of ideas. And I said it maybe this time last year, or maybe even a bit earlier, where songs that will be on the record, we've already written. We just don't know it yet. They're just kind of, like, in an iPhone recording somewhere. And that's always the kind of way. It could be kind of, like, just a lyric or kind of a guitar part, or it could be a synth part. It could be anything. It's just sat somewhere.

And a lot of the writing comes from listening back to kind of, like, jams we've had. So there's not kind of that pressure of, 'Now you're doing it.' And there's also songs on the record — a song in particular — which we started writing in a previous studio session. So you never know when ideas are going to come. That's kind of one of the exciting parts as well, where you never know when it's going to come, [wording unclear]. So you could be having the worst day in the studio, but if there's 30 seconds of a good idea at the end, you could get to run with that, which is really fun.

Sure. And that's a good reminder, I suppose, to keep showing up, even if you're not feeling it.

Normally when you're feeling it, unfortunately.

Yeah, unfortunately, that's so true. Every time someone's like, 'I feel a bit tired. Should we just go home?' we're like, 'No, because this is when the good stuff normally comes.'

[Unclear audio at 00:06:35–00:09:39]

[Unclear audio at 00:09:43–00:10:09]

So you were saying you want to do your best, which is a good sign, I think. If you didn't care about what was coming out at this stage, probably, you know, do something else.

Secret Love, for me, to my eyes, is kind of the broadest, most dynamic of your three albums, and also the most melodic, and has some really sort of pretty moments. Were you conscious of not limiting yourselves in terms of the sorts of song ideas you would explore?

I think maybe, yeah. But I think it's interesting. I think we never really think about that, I guess. We have such a specific sound, but that feels like that's kind of come about just because of who we each are, rather than something really conscious that we're trying to do. It does feel like sometimes we write things that don't really sound like us, but then somehow they always come around and end up sounding like Dry Cleaning.

We had days where Tom would just bring in a keyboard and not play guitar at all, and there's a song called I Need You that came from a day like that. And I don't know, it feels like that would break down a lot of what we sound like in a way, but it kind of still didn't. Lewis was saying the other day that maybe the answer to why we sound like how we sound is that we're all just really stubborn.

[Unclear audio at 00:12:13–00:12:15]

And we don't move very far towards each other. We just do our own thing and kind of refuse to adapt or change, even if it would be easier if we did. Even if we all went in the direction one person's pulling in, it would make a more cohesive song; we kind of still don't do it.

[Unclear audio at 00:12:38–00:12:40]

We once had a producer who tried to get me and Tom to play in sync, and we were like, 'Why would you do that?' Everyone was really upset. Everyone was like, 'This is a horrible…'

[Unclear audio at 00:12:55–00:13:00]

So wrong.

I was thinking, in the whole Dry Cleaning project there seems to be a question of, 'Will this work?' You know, all of you doing your individual things, like you're describing. And I guess you keep finding ways for the answer to be yes. But it is not obvious who's leading. That relationship between the bass and the guitar is very lateral. It's not just open chords and root notes. It's really interesting harmony. And obviously, the way you sing and your lyrics flow — not an obvious fit for the music.

No, yeah. There's a surprising amount of space for everyone. So even though everyone's very stubborn, everyone's very respectful about giving other people space to kind of, like, explore whatever their instrument is at that time. Everyone kind of swaps roles, giving someone else the chance to do a melody, or they do the melody, or they be more rhythmic. You're kind of always jamming off each other.

So I always say that we always jam off Flo's vocals. And even if you can't really hear the words in the rehearsal, because it sounds so bad in there, you can kind of hear the rhythms of what she's saying, so you get to kind of, like, roll against that. So even though there's stubbornness, there's also a respect for boundaries, of going into other people's areas.

Flo, just to ask you about working with Cate Le Bon: you made your first couple albums with John Parish, who's no mug either, but…

[Unclear audio at 00:14:36–00:14:40]

I feel it's very cool that you work with Cate Le Bon, and from everything I've read you're very fond of her and her music and the experience of working with her. When you listen to the album, do you sort of recognise a lot of her input in it?

Totally. Doing vocals with her was such a great experience. We kind of did them on our own. She sort of shooed everyone out of the studio, and we would spend the mornings, for about three or four hours every morning, doing vocals. So doing, say, three takes of a song and then listening through to them all in the control room and kind of choosing, you know, comping them together sort of thing.

And that was such a great experience because she has a very good mix of kind of that fondness for detail, but also not having too much patience for being really pernickety about things. I can get so tied up in tiny, tiny, tiny details that it's not very helpful. And she's really good at saying, 'Now, that'll do,' at the right moment. Or also with a vocal that's imperfect, she puts a lot of value on that.

So she kind of changes her dial in a way, from looking at tiny, tiny details, but also really broad strokes as well, which makes for very human-sounding records, I think. Whereas I can just focus down to a level that's a bit crackers. So I think we were a good foil for each other in that way. And also she just cared so much about the emotional quality of the performances, which is a thing that's really important to me in the kind of fairly small spectrum that I operate in.

She really cared about that, the sort of intensity of certain parts, but also when it's more about rhythm rather than emotion. She was just really attuned to all of that. Didn't really have to explain any of that. And yeah, it was just great. I could do vocals with her all day, every day. It was great. It was really good.

It's also worth saying that this didn't happen with John, because with John we recorded almost everything live together. But so often when you're in a studio, you will spend so much time tracking everything. You'd be like, 'Cool, so we've got about 10 minutes left today. Should we go do the vocals?' And that would be it, kind of like, yeah, at the last minute, which is such a huge part, such an important part.

Yeah, that happens across the board, doesn't it? That's just a music thing. Vocals are always last, and for good reasons, but also, yeah, it's a bit scary, I guess.

The same was with John. We would sit there. He had a lot of time for my attention to detail, which I love him forever for. He was up for listening to three different versions of the word Armani or whatever. He was up for that, which was a lot of words that he'd probably never heard in songs before. So, you know, maybe, who knows.

They did tease that they’ll probably be in Australia around June, maybe coming back to the Triple R performance space.
